guide.title: Heat-Related Illness
guide.lead: Mental status separates the mild from the deadly. A hot patient who is confused has heat stroke until proven otherwise: cool them hard and fast, on scene, before you transport. Antipyretics don't work in heat illness.

sections.title: Heat stroke?
sections.question: Hot environment or exertion, and any change in behaviour, confusion, seizure or coma?
sections.yes: Heat stroke: cool first, transport second. Aim to get the core below 39 °C within 30 minutes of collapse.
sections.no: Heat exhaustion or cramps: shade, lie down, remove excess clothing, oral fluids with salt, watch for change.

sections.title: Heat illness ladder
rows: Rest, stretch, oral fluids with electrolytes
Weak, dizzy, nauseated, sweating, fast pulse; normal mental status; core under 40 °C
Shade, lie flat, cool, oral fluids; IV if vomiting
Core usually above 40 °C (104 °F) with confusion, seizures or coma; skin may be dry or still sweating
Immediate aggressive cooling; airway, glucose, rapid transport after cooling

steps.title: Exertional (young, exercising)
steps.text: Cold-water immersion up to the neck – the fastest method. Stir the water; protect the airway.

figures.alt: An athlete immersed to the neck in a tub of ice water at a sports field, one rescuer supporting the head and stirring the water, another holding a rectal thermometer readout.

steps.title: No tub?
steps.text: Rotate ice-water-soaked towels over the whole body, or tarp-assisted cooling. Ice packs to neck, armpits and groin are an add-on only.

steps.title: Classic (older, during heat waves)
steps.text: Evaporative cooling: strip, mist with water, fan hard; ice packs; cold IV fluids per protocol.

figures.alt: An older patient on a stretcher stripped to underwear, being misted with a spray bottle while a fan blows across, ice packs at the neck, armpits and groin.

steps.title: Stop at 39 °C
steps.text: Remove from the water at about 39 °C (102 °F) to avoid overshoot; keep monitoring – temperature can rebound.

steps.title: Measure properly
steps.text: Rectal temperature is the reliable field core measure; oral, ear and skin readings underestimate.

sections.title: Don't
items: Give acetaminophen or ibuprofen: the set point is normal, so they don't help
Delay cooling to transport an exertional heat stroke when you can cool on site

sections.title: Watch for
items: Risk: older adults, infants, heat waves without air conditioning
Medicines: anticholinergics, antihistamines, diuretics, beta-blockers, antipsychotics, stimulants
Confused runner with normal temperature who drank a lot: exercise-associated hyponatremia – no free water, check sodium in hospital
Drug-induced hyperthermia: MDMA, cocaine, serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome

items.label: Sinus tachycardia
items.sub: Expected in heat illness; a slowing rate with confusion is worrying.

quiz.q: Football player collapses in humid heat: confused, combative, sweating, core temperature 41.1 °C (106 °F). Diagnosis and action?
options: Heat stroke: cold-water immersion on scene, then transport
Heat exhaustion: shade and oral fluids
quiz.explanation: Sweating doesn't rule out exertional heat stroke.

quiz.q: Older woman in a hot flat during a heat wave: confused, hot dry skin, on a beta-blocker. Why is she at risk?
options: Age and medicines impair heat loss and the heart's response
Dry skin means she's well hydrated
Heat stroke is milder in older adults
quiz.explanation: Classic heat stroke: evaporative cooling and rapid transport.

quiz.q: During cooling, a runner's core temperature falls to 39 °C. Next?
options: Stop active cooling, keep monitoring for rebound, transport
Cold-water immersion is the gold standard for exertional heat stroke
Ice packs on the chest are enough

quiz.q: What separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
quiz.explanation: Any CNS change in a hot patient means heat stroke.

quiz.q: Heat stroke is usually a core temperature above:
The most reliable field measure of core temperature is:
Why don't antipyretics help in heat stroke?
options: The hypothalamic set point is normal; the body is overwhelmed by heat

quiz.q: Marathon runner: confused, vomiting, temperature 38.3 °C, drank water at every station. Suspect:
quiz.explanation: No free water; hospital for sodium measurement.

options: Rest, stretching and oral electrolyte fluids

flashcards.question: Four ways the body loses heat
flashcards.answer: Conduction, convection, radiation, evaporation. Evaporation of sweat dominates in heat and exercise and fails in high humidity.

flashcards.question: Heat exhaustion vs heat stroke
flashcards.answer: Mental status. Exhaustion: alert, sweating, core under 40 °C. Stroke: confusion, seizures or coma, core usually above 40 °C (104 °F).

flashcards.question: Heat stroke priorities
flashcards.answer: Cool first, transport second: below 39 °C within 30 minutes of collapse. Airway, glucose, monitor; stop cooling at about 39 °C.

flashcards.question: Exertional vs classic heat stroke
flashcards.answer: Exertional: young, active, rapid, often sweating – cold-water immersion. Classic: older adults and infants in heat waves, slower, often dry skin – evaporative cooling.

flashcards.question: Heat cramps
flashcards.answer: Painful spasms from salt and fluid loss with heavy sweating. Rest, stretch, oral electrolyte fluids.

flashcards.question: Medicines that raise heat risk
flashcards.answer: Anticholinergics and antihistamines (less sweating), beta-blockers, diuretics, antipsychotics, stimulants (cocaine, MDMA).

flashcards.question: Malignant hyperthermia vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome
flashcards.answer: MH: rapid, after volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine – dantrolene. NMS: days to weeks after antipsychotics – rigidity, fever, confusion, unstable vital signs.

flashcards.question: No antipyretics in heat stroke
flashcards.answer: They lower a raised set point in fever. In heat stroke the set point is normal, so they do nothing and may harm the liver.

critical.scenario: Hot, humid afternoon practice: a 17-year-old lineman collapsed in the third hour. Confused and combative, hot sweaty skin, HR 140. The trainer has a cold-water tub on the sideline.
critical.question: Use the tub?

options.t: Yes: exertional heat stroke – immerse to the neck now, stir, protect the airway, check rectal temperature, remove at about 39 °C, then transport
No: transport first and cool in hospital
options.f: Delay to cooling is what kills.

options.t: Ice packs to the armpits only

critical.kpi: Initiates on-scene cold-water immersion for exertional heat stroke

critical.scenario: 75-year-old in a flat without air conditioning for 3 days of heat: confused, hot dry skin. Takes a diuretic and diphenhydramine for sleep.
critical.question: Type of heat stroke and management?

options.t: Classic heat stroke: strip, mist and fan, ice packs, cold IV fluids per protocol, airway and glucose, rapid transport
Heat exhaustion: oral fluids at home

critical.explanation: Age, the diuretic and the anticholinergic all impair heat loss.
critical.kpi: Recognizes classic heat stroke and risk factors

critical.scenario: Warm 10 km race: a 34-year-old collapses near the finish, confused, nauseated and vomiting; skin clammy; rectal temperature 38.3 °C. Friends say he drank at every station 'to be safe'.
critical.question: What do you suspect?

options.t: Exercise-associated hyponatremia: no free water, check glucose, oxygen, IV access, rapid transport for sodium measurement

critical.explanation: Confused and hot = heat stroke; confused and not hot after over-drinking = think sodium.
critical.kpi: Differentiates exercise-associated hyponatremia from heat stroke
